title: Summarize many rows

outcomes.can: Choose between counting rows and counting values that are present.
Predict how missing values affect an average.
Predict what aggregates return when no row passes the filter.
Read the error from mixing a plain column with an aggregate.
Summarize the rows that pass a filter.

intro: So far every result row came from one table row. An aggregate function turns many rows into one value: a count, a total, an average. This module covers the five common ones and the difference between counting rows and counting values.

steps.title: Many rows, one value
steps.text: An aggregate function takes a whole column of values and returns one. count(*) counts rows. sum(stock) adds values up. avg(price) is the average, min and max are the smallest and largest. A query whose SELECT list holds only aggregates returns exactly one row. WHERE is applied first, so the aggregates see only the rows that passed it. count has three forms. count(*) counts rows. count(column) counts the rows where that column is not NULL. count(DISTINCT column) counts the different values.

steps.title: Two kinds of count
steps.text: One product, the Gift Card, has no category. Predict the first two numbers.

steps.title: Rows against values
steps.text: There are 24 product rows, so count(*) is 24. count(category_id) skips the one row where category_id is NULL and gives 23. min and max look at every price and return 14.50 and 1649.00. All four answers sit in a single result row.

steps.title: Aggregates skip NULL
steps.text: sum, avg, min and max ignore NULL values. For avg that changes the answer, because a skipped row does not count toward the number it divides by. avg(bonus_pct) is the average among employees who have a bonus. To count the others as 0, give them a value first: avg(COALESCE(bonus_pct, 0)).

steps.title: Two averages
steps.text: 15 of the 24 employees have a bonus_pct. Predict which average is larger.

steps.title: What each average divides by
steps.text: avg_bonus is 12.33: the 15 known percentages added up and divided by 15. avg_all is 7.71: the same total divided by 24, because COALESCE turned the nine missing values into 0. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions, so decide which one the request means.

steps.title: No rows at all
steps.text: No product has category 99. Predict the two values.

steps.title: Zero rows still give one row
steps.text: The result still has one row. count(*) of nothing is 0. sum of nothing is NULL, not 0, because there were no values to add. The same holds for avg, min and max. Wrap the sum in COALESCE when a report needs 0.

steps.title: A column beside an aggregate
steps.text: This query asks for a product name next to the highest price. Read it before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 42803 says the column must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function. max(price) produces one value for the whole table, but name has 24 values, and SQL will not guess which one you want. The next module introduces GROUP BY, and a later one shows how to get the row that holds the maximum.

steps.title: Count the customers with an email
steps.text: The starter counts rows twice. Change one count so it counts emails.

steps.title: Summarize what is on sale
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Three aggregates, one filter.

choices.feedback: count(category_id) skips the row whose category_id is NULL.
count(*) counts every row. count(category_id) counts only the rows that have a category.
count(*) counts rows whatever they contain, so it is 24.

questions.prompt: Which is larger, avg_bonus or avg_all?

choices.feedback: It divides the total by the 15 employees who have a bonus. avg_all divides the same total by all 24.
Counting the missing values as 0 adds nothing to the total but raises the number it is divided by.
avg skips NULL, so the two versions divide by different numbers.
sum over no rows is NULL. Only count returns 0.
A query with only aggregates always returns one row.
count of nothing is 0. sum of nothing is NULL.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.text: It returns the most expensive product and its price.
choices.feedback: max(price) says nothing about which row's name to show.

choices.text: PostgreSQL reports an error on line 1.
choices.feedback: name has many values and max(price) has one, so the two cannot share a row (42803).

choices.text: It returns 24 rows, each with the highest price.
choices.feedback: An aggregate collapses the table to one row. A plain column beside it is an error.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one aggregate each. They do not compare counting rows with counting values.
